messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Kwame is a 47-year-old park ranger who has not spoken to his sister in eighteen months. She lives two hours away, and he used to see her every few weeks, but after he stopped answering her calls and eventually changed his number, she gave up. He knows she must think he is angry with her. He is not angry. He is afraid that if he lets anyone close, they will see what he did—or rather, what he failed to do—and he will see it reflected back in their eyes. That is what he cannot bear.

The event that undid him happened six years ago, when he was still working as a ranger in a large national park in a country that had descended into civil war. He had taken the job partly because he loved the quiet of the bush, the long days alone on patrol, the sense of being a steward of something ancient and wild. Then the armed groups moved through, and the park became a battleground. One afternoon his patrol vehicle was ambushed. He and three colleagues took cover in a shallow ravine as gunfire raked the treeline. One of the men, a younger ranger named Joseph, was hit and bleeding. Kwame wanted to drag him to safety, but another colleague yelled at him to stay down, that moving would get them all killed. He stayed down. Joseph died. Later that evening, as the shooting stopped and the sky turned orange from burning villages on the horizon, Kwame helped the survivors walk out. He has never been able to forget the colour of that sky, how the flames painted the acacia trees, or the way Joseph’s breath had gurgled and stopped. He also cannot forget that he did not try. He had followed an order, and that order had cost a life. In the weeks after, he told himself he had no choice, that anyone would have done the same. But the feeling never left—that he had betrayed something essential, that he had acted against the person he believed himself to be. That is the violated value that lives inside him now: he was supposed to protect, and instead he protected himself.

Returning to the United States did not help. He had been born in the U.S. but had spent most of his adult life abroad, and coming back felt like stepping into a world that had no understanding of what he carried. He found work as a park ranger in a state forest in the Midwest, thinking the familiar rhythms of the job might restore him. Instead, everything about the work became a trigger. The smell of pine after rain reminded him of the ravine. The sight of a campfire sent his heart racing so violently that he once dropped a full bucket of water and stood frozen, expecting the crackle of gunfire. He began taking routes that avoided the picnic areas where people cooked, and eventually he requested a transfer to a desk job. His supervisor, a well-meaning woman named Diane, noticed his performance slipping and called him in for a meeting. She told him he seemed distracted, asked if he was okay, and suggested he take some time off. Kwame heard her words as an accusation. *You are failing. You are not good enough. You let people down.* He did not return to work after that meeting. He filed for medical leave and has not been back since.

The isolation became total. He stopped answering the phone. He stopped going to the grocery store during daylight hours, choosing instead to slip in at 2 a.m. when the aisles were empty. He kept the blinds drawn and the television off. He drank, not every night but often enough that the empty bottles accumulated beside the recycling bin until he was too ashamed to put them out. He also took the sleeping pills his doctor had prescribed, sometimes more than the recommended dose, because the alternative was lying awake in the dark with the images. Sleep, when it came, was shallow and broken, and he often woke with a start, his hand reaching for a weapon that was not there.

He has come to believe that he is fundamentally set apart from other people now, that there is a line drawn around him that no one can cross. When he sees a police officer or a soldier in uniform, he feels a surge of adrenaline and a need to leave immediately. He cannot explain why exactly—it is not that he fears them, but that they remind him of the men with guns who passed through the park, of the chaos and the helplessness. He avoids the news for the same reason. He avoids his own reflection, because when he looks at himself he sees a man who should have died in that ravine and did not, a man who let someone else take the bullet.

The final straw came last month, when his landlord left a note under his door saying the building’s fire alarm system would be tested the following Tuesday. Kwame read the word “fire” and felt his chest seize. He spent the next three days in a state of hypervigilance, unable to relax even in his own apartment, pacing from window to door, convinced that something terrible was about to happen. When the alarm did go off, he did not leave his apartment. He sat on the floor with his back against the wall and waited for it to stop, his hands shaking, his breath shallow. That was the moment he realised he could not do this alone anymore. He called a veterans’ crisis line, though he was never in the military. The woman on the other end listened and gave him the number of a therapist who specialises in trauma. He has an appointment next week. He is terrified that she will look at him and see a coward, the same way he sees himself. But he is also tired—so tired—of living behind drawn blinds, waiting for a fire that is already inside him.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Threat in Delays: The vignette does not illustrate a situation where the patient assumes something bad when something takes longer than expected.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
